title: Aftermath and Postcards
premise: Coral Nystrom has spent six years mailing postcards to a house that burned down, addressed to her brother Anders, whose death she cannot narrate and therefore cannot mourn. When Edda Vask, the last fluent speaker of a dying language, asks Coral to become her final student before winter takes her memory entirely, Coral discovers the lessons are less about vocabulary than about confession — Edda insists every word be learned through a story never yet told aloud. As Coral's fluency grows, so does her inventory of unsaid things, until she must finally speak the truth about the fire: that Anders set it himself, and that Coral watched him do it and said nothing. The novel ends with Edda's death in early spring, Coral delivering a eulogy half in the dying tongue, and one last postcard — this time with a return address.
about_author: Rosalind Pemberton is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing undelivered letters in a municipal records office. She writes about the machinery of silence — how families store what they cannot say, and what happens when the storage fails.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. We meet her ritual: Sunday postcards to a burned address, each one logging something she didn't say — to Anders, to her mother, to the insurance investigator. The emotional beat is controlled loneliness disguised as routine; the reader senses the postcards are prayers she doesn't believe in.

chapters.title: Return to Sender, Address Unknown
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. A postal worker, Marisol, finally asks why Coral keeps sending mail to a vacant lot. Coral deflects, but that night she rereads six years of carbon copies of her own cards and notices they've grown shorter — as if the unsaid things are running out. Beat: dread beneath order.

chapters.title: The Woman Who Outlived Her Language
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. At the library where Coral volunteers, she encounters Edda Vask, an elderly woman reading a dictionary no one else can use. Edda announces, without preamble, that she needs one final student before her memory goes. Beat: reluctant fascination; Coral feels seen and threatened at once.

chapters.title: First Lesson: The Word for Leaving
chapters.summary: Coral's POV, first lesson at Edda's kitchen table. Edda teaches through stories, not lists — the word for 'leaving' requires the story of someone who left. Coral gives a safe, false anecdote. Edda's look says she knows. Beat: the first crack in Coral's careful surface.

chapters.title: Photographs of a Stranger
chapters.summary: Alternating POV begins: brief passages from young Anders's perspective in the months before the fire. He is funny, restless, increasingly desperate. Coral finds a box of his photographs and cannot reconcile the stranger in them with her inventory. Beat: grief destabilized by new information.

chapters.title: Edda's Rule
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Edda sets terms: no notebooks, no recordings — the language lives only if carried in a person. Coral, an archivist's daughter of habit, panics at the idea of unrecorded knowledge. Beat: conflict between preservation and possession; Coral realizes she hoards words like debts.

chapters.title: What the Fire Report Didn't Say
chapters.summary: Anders's POV (past). The night of the fire approaches in fragments: a job lost, a debt, a plan he tells no one. Coral, in present day, requests the official fire report and finds a page missing. Beat: rising tension — the record itself has been edited, and Coral suspects by whom.

chapters.title: Second Lesson: The Word for Blame
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Edda teaches 'blame' through a story of her own — a sister she denounced during an occupation, who died in custody. It is the first time Edda confesses anything. Beat: mutual exposure; Coral understands the lessons are confessional booths, not classrooms.

chapters.title: Marisol Reads One
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV, the only chapter not Coral's or Anders's. She admits she has been reading the postcards for years, unable to deliver them but unable to discard them. She writes back to the return address for the first time. Beat: unexpected grace; Coral receives a reply to six years of silence.

chapters.title: The Missing Page
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. She confronts her mother, Helen, about the missing report page. Helen's composure fractures just enough to reveal she removed it — to protect Coral, she claims. Beat: power inverted; the archivist of unsaid things learns her mother kept a fuller archive all along.

chapters.title: Third Lesson: The Word for Witness
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Edda teaches 'witness' — a word that grammatically requires both the event and the failure to act. Coral practices sentences she cannot finish. That night she dreams the fire accurately for the first time. Beat: the past pressing through the present; memory becoming unbearable precision.

chapters.title: Anders's Plan
chapters.summary: Anders's POV (past), fullest chapter of his voice. We see the arson take shape — insurance, desperation, a promise that no one will be hurt. He asks Coral, without asking, to cover for him. Her silence is his permission. Beat: tragic inevitability; love curdling into complicity.

chapters.title: Helen's Version
chapters.summary: Helen's POV, present day. She tells Coral what she actually knew: she suspected Anders, said nothing, and removed the report page to keep Coral's silence buried too. Mother and daughter recognize each other as fellow keepers. Beat: bitter communion; the family's whole architecture of silence exposed.

chapters.title: Fourth Lesson: The Word for Forgiveness
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Edda reveals the word for forgiveness has no passive form — it cannot be received, only performed. Edda's memory is visibly failing now, losing mid-story. Beat: urgency doubles; the student may soon know more than the teacher, and time is audibly running out.

chapters.title: The Fire, Told Aloud
chapters.summary: Coral's POV, climax of the confession arc. At Edda's table, Coral tells the whole story in the dying language, badly, haltingly — that Anders set the fire, that she watched, that her silence made her guilty. Edda does not absolve her; she simply answers in kind with her own worst truth. Beat: catharsis without comfort.

chapters.title: Winter Takes Its Inventory
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Edda declines sharply; hospital, then home hospice. Coral visits daily, now teaching Edda her own stories back to her — the student becomes the archive. Beat: tender reversal; grief arriving in installments while its subject still breathes.

chapters.title: Marisol's Lot
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She takes Coral to the burned lot, where daffodils have come up wild. Marisol confesses she almost mailed the years of cards to the city incinerator once, and couldn't. Beat: quiet solidarity between two women who keep what others would discard.

chapters.title: The Last Fluent Speaker
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Edda, lucid one final evening, formally names Coral a speaker of the language — a ceremony of three sentences. She makes Coral promise not to preserve it but to spend it, wastefully, on living people. Beat: inheritance as burden and gift; the weight becomes Coral's.

chapters.title: Eulogy in Two Tongues
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Edda dies in early spring. At the funeral, Coral delivers the eulogy half in English, half in the dying language, and publicly says Anders's name and the truth of the fire for the first time among family. Beat: climax resolved into exposure; mourning and honesty fused at last.

chapters.title: Reading the Cards Backward
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. She rereads six years of postcards in reverse, watching her silences shrink toward the fire. With Marisol, she burns them — deliberately, witnessed, unlike Anders's fire. Beat: ritual release; destruction chosen rather than suffered.

chapters.title: A Return Address
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. She writes one final postcard to Anders — honest, short, signed — and keeps it in her own mailbox instead, addressed to herself. She begins answering Marisol's letters. Beat: turning outward; the inventory of unsaid things finally open for withdrawal.

chapters.title: First Lesson, Given
chapters.summary: Coral's POV, final chapter. A stranger — a linguistics student who heard about Edda — knocks on Coral's door asking about the language. Coral puts the kettle on and begins, as Edda did, with a story never yet told aloud. Beat: cyclical resolution; the last speaker is no longer the last.
